title: Federal Reserve Proposes Risk-Based AML/CFT Program Rules for Banks: Focus on Higher-Risk Customers, FinCEN Priorities in Risk Assessments, and Enforcement Reserved for Significant Failures
summary: On July 7, 2026 the Federal Reserve Board asked for public comment on a proposal to amend Regulation H so that banks it supervises run risk-based anti-money-laundering and countering-the-financing-of-terrorism programs that incorporate FinCEN priorities, with enforcement generally reserved for significant or systemic implementation failures and comments due September 8, 2026.
description:
On July 7, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. Eastern time, the Federal Reserve Board announced that it was requesting public comment on a proposal to amend its requirements for the anti-money-laundering and countering-the-financing-of-terrorism (AML/CFT) programs that banks it supervises must maintain. The Federal Register notice, titled Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Programs, is dated July 9, 2026. This article draws on the Board's press release and on a law-firm analysis of the proposal in the National Law Review. It covers what those sources say and states where they are silent. The Board's press release does not give the vote tally or a detailed comparison with the current rule.

What the proposal would do

According to the Board, the changes are intended to match AML program proposals issued separately by other agencies. The analysis names them as the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the National Credit Union Administration. The analysis notes that FinCEN's proposed program revisions are complementary to the Fed's and that the proposals arise under separate authorities, and it does not say whether they form a joint action. The Fed's proposal would amend Regulation H, which covers membership and related requirements for state member banks, to implement provisions of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020.

The press release summarises three main changes. First, banks would focus their AML resources on the basis of risk, giving more attention to higher-risk customers and activities. Second, banks would incorporate FinCEN's AML priorities into their risk assessment processes. Third, once a bank has an AML program in place, the Board would concentrate its supervision and enforcement on significant failures to implement that program.

Program requirements

The National Law Review analysis adds detail on what a program must contain. Banks must maintain effective AML/CFT programs designed to identify, assess and mitigate money laundering, terrorist financing and other illicit finance risks. The risk assessment must cover products, services, distribution channels, customers and geographic locations, and must incorporate the applicable FinCEN AML/CFT priorities. Banks must direct more attention and resources to higher-risk customers and activities, and must update the assessment promptly when significant changes affect their risk profile.

The familiar core elements remain. These are ongoing customer due diligence, independent testing, employee training, and a designated AML/CFT officer who is located in the United States. The written program may be approved by the bank's board of directors, an equivalent governing body or appropriate senior management.

The supervisory approach

The most consequential sentence in the proposal may be the one about enforcement. Once a bank has properly established its program, the analysis says, the Board generally would reserve AML/CFT enforcement or significant supervisory actions under the program rule for significant or systemic implementation failures. In practice this signals that minor or isolated shortcomings would be less likely to trigger formal action under the program rule. The analysis does not define significant or systemic failures, and neither source gives examples, so how that line is drawn would be a matter for the final rule and supervisory practice. The word generally also leaves room for exceptions.

Governor Michael Barr issued a separate statement on the proposal, which the Board's release links to but which was not reproduced in the sources used here, so this article does not describe it.

Timeline and how to comment

The Federal Register notice says comments are due 60 days after publication. The National Law Review gives the date as September 8, 2026. For reference, 60 days after July 9 falls on September 7, which is the Labor Day holiday in 2026, so a September 8 deadline is consistent with that calculation; this is calculated here and is not stated by the sources. Comments can be submitted through a portal on the Federal Reserve's website, where they can also be viewed. After the comment period the Board would consider the feedback before deciding whether to finalise the rule. The sources give no timeline beyond the comment deadline.

What it means for banks and customers

For banks supervised by the Fed, the practical work would be to review their risk assessments against FinCEN's priorities, check that higher-risk activities receive proportionately more resources, and confirm that governance, testing and training meet the requirements. Smaller banks that run uniform programs might need to show more explicitly why they allocate resources as they do.

For customers, a risk-based approach means that people and businesses assessed as higher risk could face more questions and documentation, while others could see lighter-touch checks. The sources do not describe consumer effects, so that is a general consequence of the stated approach rather than something they say.

What is not known

The proposal is not final. The sources do not say how the rule differs in detail from the current one, do not quantify cost savings and do not describe the content of FinCEN's priorities. Banks and observers will likely comment on how significant or systemic failures should be defined. Anyone affected should read the Federal Register notice. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Federal Reserve Board (press release of July 7, 2026), with National Law Review analysis
key_points: The Board announced the proposal on July 7, 2026; the Federal Register notice is dated July 9, 2026, and comments are due September 8, 2026, 60 days after publication.
The proposal would amend Regulation H, implement provisions of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, and align with related proposals from FinCEN, the OCC, the FDIC and the NCUA.

Banks would have to base risk assessments on their products, services, distribution channels, customers and geographies, incorporate FinCEN's AML/CFT priorities, direct more attention to higher-risk customers and activities, and update assessments promptly when their risk profile changes.

Core elements stay: ongoing customer due diligence, independent testing, employee training and a designated AML/CFT officer located in the United States, with the written program approved by the board, an equivalent body or senior management.
Once a program is properly established, the Board would generally reserve enforcement or significant supervisory action under the program rule for 'significant or systemic implementation failures'.
why_it_matters: Anti-money-laundering compliance is one of banks' largest regulatory costs. The proposal says banks should concentrate effort where the risk is highest and be judged mainly on serious failures, which would change how examiners and compliance teams spend their time, although it is only a proposal and the final rule may differ.

title: Fed's Bowman Introduces the FSB's Draft 'Sound Practices' for Responsible AI Adoption: Governance Scaled to Materiality, a Lighter Touch for Low-Risk Uses and Comments Shaping a Final Report for the G20
summary: In opening remarks on July 7, 2026, Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman presented the Financial Stability Board's consultation report on sound practices for responsible AI adoption, saying governance should scale with materiality, lower-risk uses deserve a lighter supervisory touch, smaller institutions need proportionate guidance and a final report goes to the G20 later in 2026.
description:
On July 7, 2026, Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman gave opening remarks at a virtual outreach event held by the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the international body that coordinates financial regulation among major economies. The event concerned the FSB's consultation report, Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence. Bowman chairs the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, which oversaw the work. This article is based on the text of her remarks as published by the Federal Reserve. It is important to be clear about what the remarks are: an introduction to an FSB consultation document, delivered in Bowman's capacity as committee chair, and not a new Federal Reserve rule or supervisory guidance. She said her views were her own and not necessarily those of the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.

The work behind the report

Bowman thanked Hern Shin Ho of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, who led the work stream, along with FSB Secretariat staff and colleagues at the U.S. Treasury and the Securities and Exchange Commission. The report is meant to help financial institutions adopt and use AI responsibly. It does so by describing how institutions, including banks, are already managing AI risks, with the stated goal of responsible innovation. It includes examples and in-depth case studies showing governance and controls that may suit different situations.

Practices, not prescriptions

A central message is that the report is not a checklist. Bowman said that the practices in it are not the only way to adopt and use AI responsibly. That matters because the document, as a collection of observed practices, could be read as an expected standard. Her remarks position it as a menu of approaches that institutions can adapt, and she asked respondents to say where the practices might be too prescriptive.

Materiality should set the level of control

The most concrete part of the remarks concerns how much governance an AI use should attract. Bowman said institutions should be specific about how they use AI and whether that use is material to their operations or to their legal and regulatory obligations. The actual use, and its materiality, should guide the type and intensity of governance and controls for each deployment. As an illustration of the principle, and not an example from the speech, a tool that helps draft internal summaries would warrant less oversight than one that makes credit decisions.

The corollary, in her words, is that lower-risk uses should receive a lighter supervisory and regulatory touch. That is a statement of approach from a senior supervisor, and it is worth noting that it was made about the FSB's consultation and not as a commitment by the Federal Reserve to specific supervisory changes.

Proportionality and smaller institutions

The report, Bowman said, focuses on proportionality. Practices that suit large, complex AI use may not fit smaller institutions with simpler uses. She said the report gives clear guidance to all institutions, including smaller ones, and she welcomed feedback on whether it strikes the right balance. She emphasised the importance of promoting innovation at financial institutions of all sizes, not just the largest. The remarks refer to smaller institutions in general and do not mention community banks by name.

The Fed's own experience

Bowman noted that the Federal Reserve has monitored banks' use of AI for nearly a decade and has seen increased use by banks of all sizes. The remarks contain no statistics, so this article cannot say how many banks use AI or for what.

What happens next

The FSB report is a consultation, so it can change. Bowman said feedback during the public comment period will inform the final report, which will be delivered to the U.S. G-20 presidency later in 2026. She asked respondents to say where the practices may be too prescriptive, where they miss differences in size, complexity or risk, where material risks may not be addressed, and where more clarity is needed.

What the remarks do not cover

The published text does not discuss model risk management or third-party risk, topics that other commentary on AI governance often covers, and it does not set out the report's detailed recommendations. Readers who want those must read the FSB consultation report itself. The remarks also do not announce any change to U.S. regulation.

What it means

For banks, insurers and other institutions, the practical takeaways are modest but clear. First, document how and where AI is used, and assess materiality. Second, scale controls to risk rather than applying one standard everywhere. Third, consider responding to the consultation if the proportionality balance matters to the institution. For customers, the remarks do not change any rights and they do not announce any new rule. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Federal Reserve Board (opening remarks by Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman, July 7, 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence concept representing AI in banking (illustrative)
key_points: Bowman spoke on July 7, 2026 at a Financial Stability Board virtual outreach event on its consultation report, Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence; she chairs the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation and said her views were her own.

The report describes how financial institutions, including banks, already manage AI risks and includes examples and case studies of governance and controls, but Bowman stressed that 'these practices are not the only way to adopt and use AI responsibly'.

She said institutions should be specific about how they use AI and whether the use is material, and that actual use and materiality should set the type and intensity of governance and controls, with lower-risk uses receiving a 'lighter supervisory and regulatory touch'.
The report focuses on proportionality, because practices suited to large, complex AI use may not fit smaller institutions, and Bowman asked for feedback on whether it strikes the right balance.
Comments will inform a final report to be delivered to the U.S. G-20 presidency later in 2026; the Fed has monitored bank AI use for nearly a decade.
why_it_matters: Regulators around the world are deciding how much AI-specific rulemaking banks and insurers should face. This speech signals a principles-based, proportionate approach from a senior U.S. supervisor in an international forum, which matters for any institution planning how to govern its AI use.

title: India Posts $4.7 Billion Current Account Surplus for April 2026
summary: The Reserve Bank of India's first monthly balance of payments release, on June 15, 2026, showed a current account surplus of $4.7 billion for April, against a $4.8 billion deficit a year earlier, helped by net services receipts of $18.6 billion and net transfers of $16.0 billion, while portfolio outflows of $8.7 billion left the overall balance in deficit.
description:
India recorded a current account surplus of $4.7 billion in April 2026, according to preliminary balance of payments data released by the Reserve Bank of India on June 15, 2026. A year earlier, in April 2025, the country had a deficit of $4.8 billion. The figures cover a single month, which is unusual for balance of payments data that were traditionally reported by quarter. This article explains what the numbers show, where the surplus came from, and why it should be read with care. It is for general information and is not investment advice.

What the RBI reported

The balance of payments records every economic transaction between India and the rest of the world. Its first part, the current account, covers trade in goods, trade in services, income earned from abroad and transfers such as money sent home by workers. The second part, the capital account, covers investment and borrowing flows. Reports on the April data said the RBI intends to publish the figures for each reference month by the 15th day, or earlier, of the second following month.

For April 2026 the current account showed a surplus of $4.7 billion. The merchandise trade deficit was $27.9 billion, slightly wider than the $27.1 billion deficit in April 2025. Imports were $72.5 billion and exports were $44.6 billion, up from $65.8 billion and $38.7 billion a year earlier. In other words, India bought more goods from abroad and sold more as well, and the gap widened modestly.

Where the surplus came from

Two items covered that goods gap. Net services receipts, which are services exports minus services imports, were $18.6 billion, compared with $15.9 billion in April 2025. Services exports were $37.0 billion and services imports were $18.4 billion. India's services sector includes information technology, business services and other professional work sold overseas, and it has long offset part of the country's goods trade deficit.

The second item was net transfers, which were $16.0 billion against $9.4 billion a year earlier. This category consists mostly of private transfers, such as remittances sent by Indians working abroad, although the reports cited here did not break it down further. Together, services and transfers added about $34.6 billion, which exceeded the goods deficit of $27.9 billion by about $6.7 billion. The reported surplus of $4.7 billion is lower than that because other items, mainly the income account, are also part of the total. The sources we reviewed do not report the income figures, so we have not stated them.

The capital account tells a different story

While the current account moved into surplus, the capital account showed a net outflow of $11.3 billion in April, compared with a net inflow of $5.3 billion a year earlier. Net foreign direct investment rose to $7.4 billion from $1.6 billion, which is the kind of long-term investment that governments generally prefer. Foreign portfolio investors, who buy shares and bonds and can move money quickly, withdrew a net $8.7 billion.

Because of that outflow, the overall balance of payments was a deficit of $6.6 billion in April, against a surplus of $0.5 billion in April 2025. This is why a current account surplus does not by itself mean that foreign exchange reserves are rising. A deficit in the overall balance is generally met by drawing on reserves or by exchange rate adjustment, and the data here do not say which happened.

The wider picture: January to March and the full year

Context from the preceding quarter helps. In the January to March 2026 quarter, India recorded a current account surplus of $7.1 billion, or 0.7% of GDP, compared with a surplus of $13.7 billion, or 1.4% of GDP, a year earlier, according to Press Trust of India reporting on RBI data. The merchandise trade deficit that quarter was $83.4 billion, up from $59.3 billion. Net services receipts were $60.4 billion, against $53.3 billion, and remittances, reported as personal transfer receipts, were $43.5 billion, against $33.9 billion.

For the full financial year 2025-26, India had a current account deficit of $25.2 billion, or 0.6% of GDP, compared with $22.9 billion, also 0.6% of GDP, in the previous year. Net foreign direct investment inflows were $6.9 billion, and foreign portfolio investors were net sellers of $16.4 billion for the year. On a balance of payments basis, foreign exchange reserves fell by $23.6 billion over the year. So the monthly surplus for April sits within a year that, taken as a whole, still ended with a small deficit.

How to read one month of data

Monthly figures can swing widely. Shipments, the timing of payments and seasonal factors all move the numbers, and the RBI labelled the April release preliminary, so it can be revised. Monthly reporting gives analysts a faster read on the economy, but it also gives them more noisy data points. A sound approach is to look at a few consecutive months, or at the quarterly total, before drawing a trend.

It also helps to separate the sources of strength. Services and remittances have been steady contributors for years and are less exposed to commodity prices than the goods trade. The reversal in portfolio flows, by contrast, is the most volatile part of the picture. The same investors who bring in money when sentiment is strong can take it out quickly when global conditions change.

Why it matters for ordinary readers

A healthy current account reduces the amount India needs to borrow from abroad, which supports the rupee and eases pressure on the cost of imports such as fuel and electronics. It does not guarantee a stable currency, because capital flows also matter. For families who receive money from relatives abroad, the rise in transfers is a sign of how large that income stream has become for the national economy.

What to watch next

Readers can follow the RBI's next monthly release for May, which would show whether the services and transfers strength continued and whether portfolio investors returned or kept selling. The RBI publishes the data on its website. This article summarizes official figures as reported and should not be taken as investment advice.
source_name: Reserve Bank of India (preliminary monthly balance of payments data, released June 15, 2026); Press Trust of India (June 8, 2026)
image_alt: Shipping and trade representing India's external accounts (illustrative)
key_points: The RBI's preliminary data for April 2026, released on June 15, showed a current account surplus of $4.7 billion, against a deficit of $4.8 billion in April 2025.
The merchandise trade deficit was $27.9 billion, but net services receipts of $18.6 billion and net transfers of $16.0 billion, up from $9.4 billion a year earlier, more than covered it.
Net foreign direct investment rose to $7.4 billion from $1.6 billion, while foreign portfolio investors pulled out a net $8.7 billion, giving a capital account net outflow of $11.3 billion.
The overall balance of payments was a deficit of $6.6 billion in April, against a surplus of $0.5 billion a year earlier.
For the January to March 2026 quarter, India reported a current account surplus of $7.1 billion, or 0.7% of GDP, while the full 2025-26 year ended with a deficit of $25.2 billion, or 0.6% of GDP.
why_it_matters: The current account shows whether India earns more from the rest of the world than it pays out, which affects the rupee, the need for foreign borrowing and the cushion against global shocks. A surplus in one month is welcome, but it is a single reading, and the swing in portfolio flows shows that the overall position can still weaken when investors withdraw money.

title: Singapore's MAS Proposes a Protected Cell Company Framework to Host Captives, Insurance-Linked Securities and Sovereign Risk Pools in One Legal Entity
summary: MAS issued a consultation paper on July 7, 2026 proposing a Protected Cell Company structure in which assets and liabilities of each cell are legally segregated, initially for captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools; the first-phase consultation closed on August 7, 2026.
description:
Singapore's financial regulator wants to make it easier to set up captive insurers, catastrophe-bond style vehicles and risk pools inside the city-state. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issued a consultation paper on a proposed Protected Cell Company (PCC) framework on July 7, 2026, according to an analysis by the law firm Rajah & Tann Asia published on July 22. The consultation closed on August 7, 2026. It is the first phase of a two-stage process: a second phase will consult on a draft PCC Act and subsidiary legislation.

A Protected Cell Company is a single corporate vehicle in which assets and liabilities are statutorily segregated, administered under common governance. The structure consists of a Core and one or more Cells. Neither the Core nor the Cells have their own legal personality. The Core administers the PCC and provides central governance, while the Cells carry on the insurance business. A PCC must always have at least one Cell. MAS's stated aims are to support alternative risk transfer, deepen Singapore's role as a global risk-management hub and reduce administrative costs.

The benefit of the structure is that a single company can host many separate arrangements without each needing its own legal entity. Under the proposal, three insurance uses are eligible at the start. The first is captive insurance, meaning an insurer owned by the business it covers; this includes dedicated captives and "rent-a-captive" arrangements in which a corporation rents a Cell rather than forming a whole company. The second is insurance-linked securities (ILS), where insurers can issue securities through separate Cells without setting up a new special-purpose vehicle for each deal. The third is sovereign risk pools, facilities that pool risks across countries or participants, for example to share the cost of natural-disaster cover.

Segregation is the core of the proposal. As described by Rajah & Tann, MAS proposes that the assets and liabilities of each Cell be segregated both from other Cells and from the Core. "Assets of the Core must not be used to discharge the liabilities of any Cell," the proposal says, and the same principle applies between Cells. Creditors can only recover from the assets of the Core or Cell they dealt with, and charges must secure only the liabilities of that same Core or Cell. Contractual terms that are inconsistent with segregation would be void. This ring-fencing is what lets investors in one Cell be confident that problems in another will not affect them.

The proposed corporate rules cover how a PCC is formed and run. Foreign entities equivalent to a PCC could re-domicile to Singapore subject to approvals under the Insurance Act, and an existing company limited by shares could convert into a PCC through a special resolution, notification of creditors and a declaration by directors that no creditor will be materially prejudiced. Governance rules include at least one Singapore-resident director, a minimum number of directors, and the use of "PCC" or "Protected Cell Company" in the name. A PCC can issue shares and debentures on behalf of the Core or a Cell, with proceeds belonging to that Core or Cell. Capital reductions and share buybacks are permitted, dividends are allowed subject to conditions, and circular shareholding within a PCC is disallowed. Rajah & Tann's summary does not specify capital requirements, so those details are not covered here.

Transparency and oversight proposals include disclosure obligations. A PCC must identify itself as such in dealings with third parties and state that assets and liabilities are segregated. Transactions between the Core and Cells, or between Cells, are allowed if necessary, at arm's length and consistent with segregation. Each PCC needs an annual audit by a registered public accountant with separate Core and Cell financial information, and the audited statements and the register of members would be publicly accessible. On insolvency, the framework is based on the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018: a Cell can be wound up separately, and a PCC can only be dissolved once it has ceased insurance business. Existing anti-money-laundering requirements for licensed insurers would apply. For tax, the PCC would be a single entity, GST would apply at the Cell level, and each Cell would be treated as a separate person for stamp duty.

Why does this matter commercially? Cell structures are common in other offshore insurance centres, and they allow smaller risk-bearers to access captive or ILS capacity at lower cost than forming a stand-alone company. Singapore already hosts a growing insurance-linked securities market and has been trying to attract insurers, reinsurers and captive owners. The source describes MAS's goals but does not provide estimates of demand or cost savings, so the commercial impact remains to be seen.

Readers should note the status. This is a consultation proposal, not law. The second phase will consult on a draft PCC Act and subsidiary legislation, and details such as capital requirements, licensing conditions and timelines were not covered in the analysis reviewed. Companies interested in using the structure should watch for the draft legislation.

If the framework is enacted, Singapore would gain a tool to compete for captive and risk-transfer business in Asia, where natural-catastrophe protection gaps are large. The sovereign risk pool use case is notable because governments in the region have sought pooled cover for disasters. The eventual draft Act will show how detailed and attractive the regime is.
source_name: Rajah & Tann Asia (analysis of the MAS consultation paper) and Monetary Authority of Singapore

key_points: The Monetary Authority of Singapore issued a consultation paper on a Protected Cell Company (PCC) framework on July 7, 2026; the first-phase consultation closed on August 7, 2026, and a second phase will consult on a draft PCC Act and subsidiary legislation.
A PCC is a single corporate vehicle with a Core and one or more Cells, where assets and liabilities are statutorily segregated; neither the Core nor the Cells have their own legal personality.
The initial insurance use cases are captive insurance (including rent-a-captive arrangements), insurance-linked securities issued through separate cells, and sovereign risk pools.

As proposed, the assets of the Core must not be used to discharge the liabilities of any Cell, and the same principle applies between Cells; contract terms inconsistent with segregation would be void.

Foreign equivalents could re-domicile to Singapore, subject to Insurance Act approvals, existing companies could convert by special resolution, and a PCC would need at least one Singapore-resident director and an annual audit with separate Core and Cell financial information.
why_it_matters: Companies and governments increasingly look beyond traditional insurance to captives and catastrophe bonds to manage large risks. A cell structure can cut the cost of setting up each arrangement, and Singapore wants to be the Asian base for that business, competing with established offshore centres.
